tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

5. Where no document speaks, the current behaviour of the code is authoritative, and a new feature follows the conventions of its sibling features (same error classes, same guards, same events).
# ADR 0011 — Moving an issue to another project

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-03-18
- Supersedes: `docs/product/issue-move-notes.md` where the two disagree.

## Context

An issue filed in the wrong project has to be re-created by hand today. The product wants a
"move to project" action. Issue numbers are allocated per project and shown as `KEY-12`, the
search index and the audit log both denormalise the project an issue belongs to, and the plan
quota on issues is counted per project. This record fixes what a move means for each of them.

## Decision

1. **A move is one operation on one issue.** The issue leaves its project and joins the target
   project of the same workspace. Its title, description, status, priority, assignee, estimate,
   due date, labels, comments and attachments are untouched. Whatever the issue is linked to is
   left as it is.

2. **Numbers belong to projects.** The moved issue receives the **next number of the target
   project**, allocated exactly as a newly created issue's would be. Its old number is **retired**:
   a number that has ever been used in a project is never issued again in that project, whether
   the issue that carried it was archived, moved away, or moved away and back. Issues created in
   the source project afterwards continue after the highest number the project has ever issued.

3. **Permission.** Moving requires being allowed to edit the issue (the same permission every
   issue edit needs) **and** being allowed to create issues in the target project (the same
   permission creating one there needs). Both are checked against the acting member; a refusal
   changes nothing. The target project's per-project issue quota applies to a move exactly as it
   applies to creating an issue there, and a refused move changes nothing either.

4. **The audit log is append-only.** Entries written before the move keep the project they were
   written under. The move itself is recorded once, under the **target** project, as the action
   `issue.moved`, naming both projects and both numbers.

5. **Everything that is indexed by project follows the issue.** After a move, searching inside
   the target project finds the issue and searching inside the source project does not; the
   boards and the issue lists of both projects reflect it immediately.

6. **Announcing.** A move publishes exactly one domain event, `issue.moved`; it is not a
   creation, an edit or an archive, and publishes none of those.

## Consequences

- `KEY-12` links to the old key stop resolving; that is the cost of per-project numbering and
  is why the audit entry carries both numbers.
- The number allocator has to remember the highest number ever issued per project rather than
  derive it from the rows that happen to be in the project.
# Moving issues between projects — product notes

_Written while scoping the "move to project" action (2026-01). Kept for history; see `docs/adr/0011-moving-issues-between-projects.md` for the current rules._

## Why

People file issues in the wrong project all the time, and re-creating one loses the comments.

## What we'd like

- A "Move to project…" entry on the issue page, offered to anyone who can see both projects.
- The issue keeps its number, so links like `PLAT-12` keep working after the move; the page
  shows both keys ("formerly PLAT-12") for a while.
- The issue's history moves with it: the activity entries it accumulated are re-filed under
  the new project, so the project's activity tab tells the whole story.
- Comments, attachments and labels come along.

## Open questions

- What if the target project already has an issue with that number? (Probably bump it.)
- Plan limits: does the target project's issue quota apply to a move? (Leaning no — it is not a
  new issue.)

/**
 * Brings `databasePath` up to date. Generated migrations win when they exist;
 * otherwise the embedded schema is pushed. Safe to run repeatedly — every
 * statement is `IF NOT EXISTS`.
 */
export async function runMigrations(
  databasePath: string = process.env.TASKFLOW_DB_PATH ?? DEFAULT_DB_PATH,
): Promise<void> {
  const absolute = resolve(process.cwd(), databasePath);
  mkdirSync(dirname(absolute), { recursive: true });

  const sqlite = new Database(absolute);
  sqlite.pragma("journal_mode = WAL");

  try {
    for (const statement of readMigrationStatements()) {
      sqlite.exec(statement);
    }
  } finally {
    sqlite.close();
  }
}

/** `pnpm db:migrate` runs this file directly; importing it must stay inert. */
if (process.argv[1]?.endsWith("migrate.ts") === true) {
  await runMigrations();
}

function readMigrationStatements(): readonly string[] {
  const dir = resolve(process.cwd(), MIGRATIONS_DIR);
  if (!existsSync(dir)) return SCHEMA_STATEMENTS;

  const files = readdirSync(dir)
    .filter((name) => name.endsWith(".sql"))
    .sort();

  if (files.length === 0) return SCHEMA_STATEMENTS;

  return files.flatMap((name) =>
    readFileSync(join(dir, name), "utf8")
      .split("--> statement-breakpoint")
      .map((chunk) => chunk.trim())
      .filter(Boolean),
  );
}

/**
 * Brings `databasePath` up to date. Generated migrations win when they exist;
 * otherwise the embedded schema is pushed. Safe to run repeatedly — every
 * statement is `IF NOT EXISTS`.
 */
export async function runMigrations(
  databasePath: string = process.env.TASKFLOW_DB_PATH ?? DEFAULT_DB_PATH,
): Promise<void> {
  const absolute = resolve(process.cwd(), databasePath);
  mkdirSync(dirname(absolute), { recursive: true });

  const sqlite = new Database(absolute);
  sqlite.pragma("journal_mode = WAL");

  try {
    for (const statement of readMigrationStatements()) {
      sqlite.exec(statement);
    }
  } finally {
    sqlite.close();
  }
}

  await runMigrations();
}

function readMigrationStatements(): readonly string[] {
  const dir = resolve(process.cwd(), MIGRATIONS_DIR);
  if (!existsSync(dir)) return SCHEMA_STATEMENTS;

  const files = readdirSync(dir)
    .filter((name) => name.endsWith(".sql"))
    .sort();

  if (files.length === 0) return SCHEMA_STATEMENTS;

  return files.flatMap((name) =>
    readFileSync(join(dir, name), "utf8")
      .split("--> statement-breakpoint")
      .map((chunk) => chunk.trim())
      .filter(Boolean),

The backend for moving an issue to another project is in. Typecheck and lint are clean, and the full suite passes (628 tests).

Where the product note and ADR 0011 disagree, I followed the ADR, since `docs/README.md` ranks ADRs above product notes. So the issue gets the target project's next number rather than keeping its old one. Its earlier audit rows keep their project and are not re-filed. The target project's quota applies to a move.

- **`moveIssueToProjectSchema` and `MoveIssueToProjectInput`**: added to `src/schemas/issue.ts` as specified.
- **`moveIssueToProject(actor, input)`**: added to `issue-service.ts` and returns the issue as stored afterwards. It checks, in this order:
  1. The actor's org scope.
  2. `issue:update` on the issue, and that the issue isn't archived.
  3. A same-project move returns the issue unchanged and publishes nothing. This check comes before the target checks, so a project already at quota doesn't refuse a no-op.
  4. The target project exists in the same workspace and isn't archived.
  5. `issue:create` on the target.
  6. The target's per-project issue quota, with the same error as creating an issue.

  Only after all of that does it write and publish `issue.moved`.
- **`issue.moved` event**: added to `TaskflowEventMap` with the payload you specified, published with the acting member as the actor.
- **`issue.moved` audit action**: added to the activity types, the zod enum that validates audit-log filters, and the label map. The listener in `activity-service.ts` records one row under the target project, with the metadata you listed.
- **Search**: a new `issue.moved` listener re-indexes the issue, so it appears in the target project's search results and drops out of the source's. Boards and lists read the table directly, so they follow without changes.

**Number allocation:** the old allocator took the highest number among the rows in a project, which would hand a moved-away number out again. I added a `project_issue_counters` table holding the highest number ever issued per project. The change touches:
- the drizzle schema in `src/server/db/schema/issues.ts`;
- the migration statements in `src/server/db/migrate.ts`;
- the seed's table cleanup;
- `issue-repository.ts`, where `nextIssueNumber` and `insertIssue` now use the counter.

The move itself runs in one transaction in the new `moveIssueToProject` repository function, so a failure leaves the issue and both counters as they were. Existing databases need `pnpm db:migrate` to create the new table. Projects with no counter row fall back to the highest existing number.

I also changed `relocateIssue`, the import tool's primitive, to record both projects' counters. That wasn't in your list, but without it the "never reissued" rule would have a gap there.

I added `tests/services/issue-service.move.test.ts` with 11 cases covering the above. No existing test needed changing.
